readerTitle: The restaurant budget that ends on opening night
caseNote: 가상 사례 (40석 레스토랑 개업, 청소 서비스 회사의 2호점) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 개업 예산은 문을 여는 날이 아니라 매출이 매달 비용을 감당하는 날까지 잡고, 느린 경우에 무엇을 할지 미리 정해 둔다.
misconception: 공사비와 장비비 견적 안에 들어오면 개업 예산은 충분하다.

sources.text: 예산과 시나리오 계획의 표준 개념 (FIN-05-01, FIN-05-03에서 다룸)

factChecks.note: 개업 비용 합계: 공사 $120k + 주방 장비 $80k + 가구·인테리어 $30k + 인허가·보증금 $20k + 초기 재고·교육 $10k = $260k. 보유 자금 $350k − $260k = $90k. 개업 비용 내역은 3번 카드 본문에 묶어서 표시했습니다.
3번 카드 합계: $260k + $60k + 예비비 $26k(공사·장비 등 개업 비용의 10%) = $346k, 보유 자금 대비 여유 $4k. 6번 카드: 느린 시나리오 $260k + $140k = $400k, 보유 자금 대비 $50k 부족(예비비 제외).

cards.title: The restaurant budget that ends on opening night
body: Maya has $350,000, a 40-seat space she loves, and a builder's quote of $260,000 for everything it takes to open.
On paper she has $90,000 to spare. She's about to sign the lease.

image.label: A restaurant owner reviewing a quote in an empty dining room
image.brief: 공사 중인 빈 레스토랑. 의자가 쌓여 있고 주인이 견적서를 들고 미소 짓는다. 견적서에 "$260,000"만 크게 보임. 벽 달력은 개업일에서 끝나 있음. 실제 브랜드나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Is Maya covered?
body: Her quote covers renovation, kitchen equipment, furniture, permits, deposits, opening stock and staff training. Rent, salaries and insurance will run about $40,000 a month once she opens.
With $350,000 in the bank, is her budget complete?

options.text: Yes. The quote is solid and she has $90,000 left over
options.feedback: The quote covers getting the doors open. It says nothing about the months when the room is half full and the $40,000 bills still arrive.

options.text: Not yet. She needs to add the months before sales cover the monthly bills
options.feedback: This is the **budget** idea at work: plan spending all the way to the goal, and the goal is a restaurant that pays for itself, not just an open one.

options.text: Almost. Add 10% to the quote for overruns and she's fine
options.feedback: A contingency protects against building surprises, which is wise. But it still stops at opening night and misses the ramp-up.

cards.title: The budget, finished.
body: The one-time costs are the part everyone sees. In her expected case, Maya also needs $60,000 to cover the gap while the room fills. Total: **$346,000**, leaving just $4,000.

breakdown.label: Ramp-up gap
breakdown.detail: Monthly bills not yet covered by sales

cards.title: An opening budget runs until the business pays for itself.
body: A **budget** is a plan for what you'll spend to reach a goal. For an opening, that goal is the month when sales cover the monthly bills.
So the budget has two halves: the one-time costs to open, and the running costs during the ramp-up. The second half is the one that's easy to forget, because no builder sends a quote for it.

image.label: Timeline: opening costs, then a ramp-up gap closing over months
image.brief: 가로 타임라인. 왼쪽 "Opening costs" 큰 블록, 개업일 표시 이후 "Ramp-up gap" 막대들이 달마다 점점 작아지다 "Sales cover the bills" 지점에서 사라짐.

cards.softwareNote: For a software launch, the ramp-up is the months of salaries and ad spend before subscriptions cover them. The same two halves apply.

cards.title: The gap depends on how fast the room fills.
body: Maya models three cases. Each month, sales leave a bit more toward her $40,000 of bills: $15,000 more in the fast case, $10,000 in the expected case, $5,000 in the slow one.
The slow case takes eight months and needs more than twice the expected gap.

groups.label: Money needed before sales cover the monthly bills

image.label: The gap depends on how fast the room fills.
image.brief: Labeled HTML chart from the lesson numbers

cards.title: The slow case doesn't fit.
body: In the slow case, Maya needs $260,000 to open plus $140,000 to get through the ramp-up: $400,000. She has $350,000. What should she do before signing?

options.text: Plan on the expected case. The slow one is just pessimism
options.feedback: That ignores the point of **scenario planning**. If the slow case happens, she runs out of money in month six with no plan.

options.text: Decide now: trim opening costs, line up a backup credit source, and set a trigger, such as dropping lunch service if month-three sales are under target
options.feedback: This is **scenario planning** at work. She can't know which case comes, but she decides her moves in advance, while she still has choices.

options.text: Delay until she has raised $430,000 to cover the slow case plus contingency
options.feedback: Very safe, but it may cost months, the space, or a share of the business. Covering the worst case fully isn't the only way to survive it.

cards.title: A cushion only works if you protect it.
body: Contingency money tends to get spent on nicer chairs during the build. Keep it in a separate account with a rule for when it can be used.
And the slow case isn't the worst case. It's a planning tool, not a promise. Pick two or three cases that would change your decisions, rather than modeling ten.

cards.title: Now it's a cleaning company.
body: Leon runs a home cleaning business and is opening a second branch in a nearby city. He needs vans, equipment and local ads. Two crews will cost wages from day one, but his schedule there starts empty. Which plan is strongest?

options.text: Budget vans, gear and ads. The first branch's profits will cover the rest
options.feedback: It skips the ramp-up half of the **budget** and quietly puts the first branch at risk if the new one fills slowly.

options.text: Budget setup plus crew wages until the schedule fills, in an expected and a slow case, with a trigger to drop to one crew
options.feedback: Both ideas at work: a **budget** that runs to self-funding, and **scenario planning** that decides the fallback in advance.

options.text: Hire no crews until the schedule is full
options.feedback: It cuts the wage risk, but he can't take bookings he can't serve. Using one crew or freelancers at first may balance both.

cards.softwareNote: A software company hiring a sales team for a new region faces the same shape: salaries start now, closed deals come months later.

cards.title: Budget to the day it pays for itself, not the day it opens.
body: Concepts used: **Budgets**, which cover the full path to the goal, and **scenario planning**, which decides your moves for a slow start before it happens.
**Try it today:** take any opening or expansion you're planning. Write the month you expect it to cover its own bills, then the month in a slow case. What would you cut first?
